Simon Baker moved to Hollywood to help his wife Rebecca Rigg become a movie star. She was the one with real acting experience. He'd never appeared in a feature film in his life. Hollywood picked him instead — he landed a deal worth over $30 million, while Rebecca later said watching it happen felt "like a slap in the face."

In the clip below, Simon explains why they moved for her career. Rebecca describes what it felt like watching him get the opportunities she'd been chasing.

1990s. Simon meets Rebecca on the Australian soap E Street. He's 22 with barely any credits. She's already the established performer.

1993. Simon wins Australia's Logie Award for Most Popular New Talent. Rebecca is still the more experienced name.

They move to Los Angeles for her shot at Hollywood. Simon has never been in a feature film.

1997. He auditions for a lead in L.A. Confidential. Guy Pearce gets it. Simon calls it devastating.

Producers offer him a small role instead. Within weeks, agencies are calling and TV offers stack up.

Rebecca watches the roles reverse. "It was a bit of a slap in the face for me."

1998. They marry. 3 children follow.

2000. Warner Bros. gives him a deal reportedly worth over $30 million. By 2011 he's making a reported $350,000 an episode.

2021. After 29 years, they split. They sell their Sydney house for nearly A$17 million — A$10.5 million more than they paid.

She went to Hollywood as the experienced one. He walked away with the $30 million career.

Did Hollywood pick the wrong actor, or did Rebecca back the right one and lose the credit for it?

🇺🇸🇮🇷 How does a new Iran war break the US economy? Oil above $100 and a Fed that keeps hiking into it

Missiles alone won’t do it, and that’s the surprising part.

Michael Lebowitz, a portfolio manager, says markets shrug at war as long as oil stays in the $ 80s, the same way they shrugged at Ukraine.

The danger starts if drones hit Gulf energy sites and crude runs past $100, because he expects the Fed to answer with hike after hike against inflation it can’t fix.

Michael on what those hikes would land on:

“And the economy I feel is kind of limping to begin with. But it’s got this huge AI crutch that makes it look great.”

So picture pricier gas, pricier loans and a wobbling AI boom all arriving together.

Who feels that first?

The family already stretched at the pump and on the credit card, long before Wall Street does. Watch the price of a barrel, because it will tell you more than any battlefield map.

@michaellebowitz @WeTheBrandon

🚨🇺🇸 Win the Senate and fire the leader? Chris Van Hollen is coming for Chuck Schumer’s job after the Democrats’ biggest night in decades

Only in Washington does the winning team hold the mutiny.

Tom Bevan of RealClearPolitics says the challenge began as a long shot and has grown into a real threat, and he doesn’t see Schumer walking off the stage by choice.

Justin Snyder, a Democratic strategist, counts about 15 senators behind Van Hollen and expects more before the secret ballot in early December.

Justin on Schumer telling everyone the race is already over:

“If you have it all wrapped up, you don’t need to say that, right?”

So does Schumer fight to the last vote, or cut a backroom deal and step aside the way Pelosi did? 

Justin expects the exit if the count gets close, and a party that just won by promising change will struggle to keep the same face out front.

Taxes that Labour have raised since the election:

1. Employer National Insurance: up from 13.8% to 15%
2. Employer National Insurance threshold: cut from £9,100 to £5,000
3. Income tax thresholds: frozen until 2031
4. Capital gains tax: up to 18% and 24%
5. Tax on selling your business: up from 10% to 18%
6. Inheritance tax on family farms
7. Inheritance tax on family businesses
8. Inheritance tax on pensions: from 2027
9. Inheritance tax thresholds: frozen until 2031
10. VAT on private school fees: 20%
11. Business rates on private schools
12. Stamp duty on second homes: up from 3% to 5%
13. Tax on savings interest: up 4 points
14. Tax on rental income: up 4 points
15. Tax on dividends: up 2 points
16. National Insurance on pension salary sacrifice: from 2029
17. Mansion tax on homes over £2m: from 2028
18. Pay-per-mile tax on electric cars: 3p a mile from 2028
19. Car tax: first-year rates doubled
20. Company car tax on double-cab pick-ups
21. Air Passenger Duty
22. Online gaming duty: up from 21% to 40%
23. Online betting duty: up from 15% to 25%
24. Tobacco duty
25. Alcohol duty
26. A new vaping tax
27. Sugar tax: extended to milkshakes
28. North Sea windfall tax: up from 35% to 38%
29. Bank surcharge: doubled from 3% to 6%
30. Business rates on large premises
31. Non-dom tax status: scrapped
32. Carried interest tax: up to 32%
33. Tax relief on business equipment: cut twice
34. Tax relief on selling to your employees: halved
35. VAT on minicab fares: from 2028
36. Import duty on small parcels

And now:
37: The Overnight Visitor Levy (aka the Holiday Tax)

When will it end?
